title: How OCD Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about actor Tony Shalub (star of Monk) and the show's name, then discuss obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD): what it is, how obsessions and compulsions work, the four obsession categories (germs, symmetry, doubt, disturbing thoughts), examples like hand washing, checking, and reporting compulsions in restaurants, links to agoraphobia and hair pulling, basketball player Chris Jackson, a 2002 case study of hypersexuality linked to OCD, and treatment via cognitive behavioral therapy (exposure and response prevention) and antidepressants. The episode closes with a sponsor line and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and Monk
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the name Monk, actor Tony Shalub, and a wedding they both attended, then transition to the episode topic of OCD.

segments.title: What OCD is and personal quirks
segments.summary: Hosts define OCD as obsessive compulsive disorder and distinguish clinical OCD from quirky habits, such as avoiding sidewalk cracks, with Chuck describing his own habits.

segments.title: Obsessions, compulsions and hand washing
segments.summary: Explanation that OCD obsessions are intrusive thoughts that feel huge, that compulsions are used to relieve them, and that people may repeat actions a set magic number of times, such as washing hands ten times or locking doors.

segments.title: Four categories and symmetry
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the four obsession categories: germs, symmetry, doubt, and disturbing thoughts. Chuck describes his need to place objects in certain spots as an example of symmetry.

segments.title: Doubt and restaurants
segments.summary: Doubt obsessions are described, including checking appliances. A New York Times writer's experience with OCD in restaurants is discussed, including checking a signed credit card receipt.

segments.title: Reporting compulsion, agoraphobia and hair pulling
segments.summary: The reporting compulsion is described using a wobbly restaurant table example. The hosts note the public embarrassment that can lead to agoraphobia and hair pulling.

segments.title: Chris Jackson and disturbing thoughts
segments.summary: Basketball player Chris Jackson is mentioned as having OCD and tying his shoes repeatedly, which made him late and affected leaving the house. Disturbing thoughts are introduced as the fourth category, and a 2002 case study linking hypersexuality to OCD is discussed.

segments.title: Treatment: CBT and exposure and response prevention
segments.summary: Hosts state OCD is treatable, with cognitive behavioral therapy as the main method, including exposure and response prevention, and sometimes antidepressants.

segments.title: Sign-off and sponsor
segments.summary: Hosts point listeners to the How Stuff Works site for more on OCD, invite email, and end with a sponsor line for a camera.
